item.title: How to Become a Tech Conference Speaker (And Why You Might Regret It)
item.content:encoded:
Originally published on 21 October 2026 at 08:05 UTC — 229 likes

So you want to be a conference speaker? Are you sure?

Recently, a few people have asked me what it's actually like to speak at tech conferences. How do you get accepted? What does preparation look like? And what happens behind the scenes? So I decided to write about it. And let me warn you: the reality isn't always pretty. In fact, after hearing about my experiences, one person has already put their conference-speaking plans on hold indefinitely. 😅

Because conferences aren't just about getting on stage and having fun. They're also about rejected abstracts, endless preparation, stress, and logistics. And is it actually worth it? Let's find out! 😉

One little disclaimer: everything I'm about to share is based on my own experiences and observations. Other speakers might have completely different perspectives, and I'd love to hear them in the comments!

Before we start, let me briefly tell you about my conference "achievements," so you know where I'm coming from. I gave various talks and workshops around 2019, then took a break for several years to focus on my professional development, occasionally running a workshop here and there.

About a year ago, I decided to get back into conference speaking seriously. Since then, I've spoken at:

JS Poland

jsday Bologna

JSNation (online)

AGNTCon + MCPCon Europe (Amsterdam)

FrontKon (Prague)

And I still have two conferences coming up this year:

iJS Munich

AI Coding Summit Berlin

I even had to turn down one invitation because I simply couldn't fit it into my schedule anymore. :( I still regret it!

I got accepted to some through CFPs, was invited to others, and got a few opportunities partly through connections (for example, because another speaker remembered me from a previous conference).

I'm not a keynote speaker. I often speak on additional tracks or in smaller rooms, and I'm perfectly fine with that. Actually, I think that's what makes my perspective interesting. I'm not a conference veteran with ten years of experience whom organizers are fighting to book.

And while I feel pretty confident about blogging these days, conference speaking still gives me a massive case of impostor syndrome. Especially since English isn't my native language. I always think nobody will ever invite me again. And somehow, people keep inviting me. 😅

Okay, so how do you actually get accepted as a conference speaker?

If you're not the face of a huge tech company, the maintainer of a famous library, or some kind of tech celebrity, your main option is to apply through a CFP ( Call for Papers ). Most major conferences accept talk proposals, so you just need to check their websites for submission deadlines.

item.title: We're Building AI to Replace Ourselves. What's the Plan?
item.content:encoded:
Originally published on 4 November 2026 at 08:06 UTC — 173 likes

Weren't we supposed to be replaced by AI by now? Or at least work less? AI agents were supposed to take over the world. So when exactly is that going to happen, and why are we still working so much?

Because we can't pretend that nothing has changed. Even at my workplace, where data security is valued above pretty much everything else, we're already using AI coding agents. Which, in my opinion, means they're basically everywhere by now.

Simple features practically write themselves, and even debugging, including in legacy applications, has become significantly easier.

And we're only at the beginning of this revolution!

A friend and colleague of mine recently encouraged me to write an article about how to get into AI before it's too late. After all, someone will have to build this revolution, right?

Soon, applications will practically write themselves. AI will even be sitting in your toilet, politely suggesting that it's time to get up before you give yourself hemorrhoids. xD So what should we do to avoid being pushed out of the job market?

Since I know a thing or two about AI agents, and I've been in this industry for quite a while, I started researching what the next few years might look like. And the longer I researched, the more pessimistic I became. Because sure, right now we have huge conferences dedicated to AI agents. We're trying to build them properly, make them secure, reliable, and so on.

But what happens in a few years, when we've solved those problems too, and an agent can spin up ten sub-agents of its own from a single prompt? Where exactly will developers fit into that picture?

(Okay, for now I still get the impression that hardly anyone even knows what tool calling or WebMCP is. 😅 But maybe that's just a matter of time?)

Okay, but there's a catch in this whole theory. Sometimes, when I hear people talking about how "AI is going to replace all of us," I feel like we're forgetting something pretty important. If a massive company can be run by just a handful of people thanks to AI, and most of the population ends up unemployed, who exactly are those companies going to sell their products to? People need to earn money to buy things, after all!

Now, let's throw all restraint out the window and go full science fiction. Imagine it's 2031. Autonomous AI agents do practically everything. Humans are left with manual jobs, like plumbers or hairdressers.

But even those people have hardly any customers, because everyone else is unemployed and desperately cutting back on unnecessary expenses.

The economy starts collapsing. People start protesting. So what do governments do? To prevent a full-blown revolt and keep themselves in power, they start introducing laws designed to bring humans back into the workforce.

Maybe in five or ten years, software engineering won't be a job for people who actually know how to program or understand the technology. Maybe it'll be something literally anyone can do.

But perhaps we should take this idea even further. Instead of throwing people out of their jobs, why not take advantage of how productive AI agents are and let people work part-time for the same salary Maybe we could work three days instead of five, and spend the rest of our time doing whatever we want: relaxing, learning new things, developing ourselves?

Oh, what a beautiful vision! Just imagine how many articles I could write. I'd finally get enough sleep. I might even find time to deal with that enormous pile of clothes sitting in my wardrobe, which currently has approximately zero priority in my life! 🤯

But there's just one tiny problem with this wonderful vision. Where is all that free time we've been promised since the invention of the steam engine? Because I'm certainly not working less!

Quite the opposite, actually. I feel like I'm working more and more, and expectations keep growing, because "AI will help you with that." And yes, some of the actual coding, the part so many of us genuinely enjoyed, has already been partially automated.

But what about everything else? The coordination, the endless meetings, the constant effort to make sure the entire project doesn't fall apart?

Don't you get the impression that because it seems like we should be able to deliver more, that's exactly what we keep trying to do? And somehow, it doesn't always work out the way we expected?

item.title: Your DEV posts have a beautiful new share card ✨
item.content:encoded:
Originally published on 27 October 2026 at 16:44 UTC — 175 likes

The image that shows up when you share a DEV post just got a brand-new look!

I got to work on forem/forem#24071 last week and I'm so excited to see it live in production:

[ ] Refactor

[x] Feature

[x] Bug Fix

[x] Optimization

[ ] Documentation Update

Articles without a cover image get a generated share image ( articles.social_image ). In the last 30 days on DEV, that was 73% of published posts. The old card had two problems:

It repeated the title. X, LinkedIn and Slack already show the title as text next to the image.

X's title label covered the byline. X overlays the post title in a dark label inset at the bottom-left of link cards, right on top of the author's name and date.

New design: the card quotes the opening of the post inside a browser-window frame over a soft mesh gradient. A byline row shows the avatar, name, date and reading time, and the community's horizontal header logo ( Settings::General.resized_logo , falling back to logo_png ) sits in the window's title bar.

One image for every platform: the card is sized so its top and bottom margins both equal X's 80px keep-clear zone.

X's title label covers only the gradient.

The card is vertically centered where nothing is overlaid (LinkedIn, Slack, iMessage, …).

A spec enforces both. No schema change and no view change.

Quote ( Images::SocialImageQuote ):

Uses top-level opening paragraphs. Skips paragraphs that are entirely italic (challenge "This is a submission for…" intros), paragraphs that repeat the title, and headings, code, images and blockquotes. Blockquotes usually quote someone else, and the card attributes the text to the author.

Joins short paragraphs until there are at least 80 characters, then cuts at the last sentence end within 180 characters, or at a word with "…".

Falls back to the title when the post has no usable paragraph.

item.title: Promise Delivered: Welcome to the DEV Hall of Fame (65 Authors, 65 Masterpieces)
item.content:encoded:
Originally published on 18 October 2026 at 10:55 UTC — 227 likes

Status: Promise delivered ✅

A little over a month ago, I published this:

Community members share hidden gem posts

The deal was simple. You pick the one article you're most proud of, not the one with the most reactions, the one you love the most. I read it and give you my honest feedback.

I expected maybe 15 or 20 replies. The thread ended up with over 250 comments.

Was it tough? Absolutely. There were evenings when my eyes desperately asked me to stop. But I read every single one.

That post had a second promise hidden at the very end: "Let's build a hall of fame of DEV's best work!"

So here it is.

Every article below was chosen by the person who wrote it. Not by an algorithm, not by a reactions count, not by me. By the author.

📌 A quick note: A few of you shared articles hosted outside DEV. I read them, but I haven't included them here. This hall only features articles published on DEV, because I can't vouch for external links, and I don't want to send readers somewhere I can't verify is safe.

📌 A quick note: A few of you shared articles hosted outside DEV. I read them, but I haven't included them here. This hall only features articles published on DEV, because I can't vouch for external links, and I don't want to send readers somewhere I can't verify is safe.

Before the tour starts, a few numbers:

65 authors, 65 masterpieces.

600+ minutes of listed reading time. That's over 10 hours, and in reality it was much more, because listed reading time is a polite lie.

The longest read: 68 minutes. It took me closer to 100.

The shortest read: 1 minute.

The oldest exhibit: published in March 2020.

The most reactions: 623.

Zero reactions: 8 articles had none when I collected them. Zero! That's exactly why this hall exists.

The exhibits are grouped into wings by theme, so you can head straight to whatever interests you most. Each exhibit has the article itself, why the author picked it (when they told me), and my take.

item.title: Your Browser Can Do WHAT?! 5 AI Features That Actually Work
item.content:encoded:
Originally published on 14 October 2026 at 07:05 UTC — 211 likes

Are AI models running directly in the browser finally good enough to use in production? Let's find out! 😉

It's been a week since my talk at FrontKon in Prague. As I mentioned before, it was fantastic! I'm adding a few photos below, just to prove that I actually speak at conferences and don't just make these things up. 😀

My talk was titled "Your Browser Is a Compute Platform (And You're Using It for Forms)" , and I showed how we can use WebAssembly and WebGPU to perform advanced computations directly in the browser. I was a little concerned to discover that, out of everyone in the audience, maybe three or four people had even heard of WebGPU! And that's a shame, because WebGPU can accelerate certain types of parallel computations by tens of times compared to CPU-based implementations.

But okay, at least the people at FrontKon know what WebGPU is now. 😁 And if you'd like a talk about this at your conference, feel free to reach out! Especially if your conference happens to take place in a particularly attractive tourist destination. 😀

After a conference, I traditionally prepare a blog post related to my talk. However, since I've already written about WebAssembly and WebGPU many times, today I'd like to approach the topic from a different angle. Namely, let's take a look at the current state of AI models running directly in the browser , which, of course, make extensive use of these technologies. 🙂

Browser-based AI models are a fascinating concept. No inference API calls. No network round trips to an AI backend. No worrying that your users will consume too many tokens, because you're not paying for them! But of course, local inference still takes time, and downloading the model in the first place can take a while.

Another advantage is that these models can work offline once they've been downloaded and cached by the browser, provided the application itself supports offline operation.

And that also brings a significant privacy benefit: inference happens directly on the user's device, so their data doesn't need to be sent to an external AI service.

However, as you can probably imagine, these are relatively small models. We're not going to run a massive frontier-scale model in a typical browser tab.

So the question is: how useful are these smaller models, really?

Some of you may remember that I experimented with browser-based AI models about a year ago. Back then, we were mostly laughing that they were a fun curiosity, but not much more than that.

But I've been following people from Hugging Face who work on Transformers.js on LinkedIn, and every now and then, their demos would appear in my feed. At first glance, some of them looked genuinely impressive. You know, practically spaceships running inside a browser. 😉

So before FrontKon, I decided to take another look at what they had to offer. And it turned out that after upgrading Transformers.js to version 4.3.1, which I used for these experiments, and trying some newer models, the results were genuinely impressive!

Of course, Transformers.js isn't the only option for running AI models in the browser. There are other libraries and runtimes, but I really like Transformers.js, and I think it's a pretty representative example of what this technology can achieve today.

At the same time, I don't work for Hugging Face, and nobody is paying me to sell you a spaceship in your browser. So I'll tell you what browser-based AI models can actually do today, what works well, and what still doesn't.

And even better, you can explore the code and try everything yourself!

GitHub: https://github.com/sylwia-lask/practical-browser-ai

Live demo: https://sylwia-lask.github.io/practical-browser-ai

If you like the project, please give it a star on GitHub. I'm collecting them! 😀

For these demos, I wanted to focus on practical applications. More specifically, I wanted to find out how we could use browser-based AI today, right now, in real production applications.

item.title: How I Feel about the Grace Hopper Celebration Getting Cancelled
item.content:encoded:
Originally published on 13 October 2026 at 14:57 UTC — 106 likes

The Grace Hopper Celebration has been around since 1994, and for a lot of people, it's the event for women in tech. It's where students land their first internships, where people find mentors and peers who look like them, and where, for a few days, being a woman in a room full of technologists is the norm instead of the exception.

AnitaB.org has cancelled this year's Celebration , which was supposed to take place in Anaheim later this month. Their statement says registrations and sponsorships came in "significantly below" expectations, and the funds needed to put on the event just weren't there.

I was supposed to attend for the first time this year and host a panel on the evolution of nontraditional career paths into tech. I was really looking forward to that conversation.

A little over two years ago, I wrote about how I felt when Women Who Code shut down , and this news brings up a lot of the same feelings.

Conferences like Grace Hopper run on company support, and that support shows up in two ways. The obvious one is sponsorship: booths, recruiting teams, and the dollars that make an event of this scale possible. The less obvious one is registrations. Between tickets, flights, and hotels, attending GHC adds up fast, and for a big chunk of attendees, it's their employer who has historically covered the cost. So when companies stop paying for their teams to attend, low registrations aren't a sign that people don't want to go. They're the same sponsorship gap, just showing up in a different line item.

When that support dries up on both fronts, even the most established event in the space can't happen.

When Women Who Code shut down, it felt like my fears of stagnancy and going backwards were being confirmed. I wish I could say things have turned around since then. Instead:

Company budgets for DEIB have continued to shrink, and "diversity" has become a word a lot of companies would rather not say out loud.

Sponsorship dollars for community events have dried up across the board.

The people these spaces serve are still tired. Being the only woman in the room hasn't gotten less exhausting just because it's gotten less fashionable to talk about.

Women Who Code and Grace Hopper were two of the biggest, most established institutions in this space. If the tech industry, which is by most measures still incredibly well-resourced, isn't investing in them , then smaller grassroots groups are in an even tougher spot.

One of my personal goals right now is to speak more, and news like this makes that feel more important than ever. If the big stages are disappearing, those of us who have a platform need to keep using it.

But you don't need a stage to make a difference. Look around at your team, your community, your classmates, and find the people who are undervalued and underrepresented. Mentor them, recommend them, amplify their work, and make sure they're heard in the rooms they're in. That kind of support doesn't need a sponsor.

Thanks for reading <3

item.title: Yes, {} + [] = 0. No, JavaScript Isn’t Broken
item.content:encoded:
Originally published on 29 October 2026 at 20:08 UTC — 170 likes

JavaScript is a legendary programming language. Created in the mid-1990s in just 10 days, it was born during the browser wars, when Netscape was trying to deliver a fatal blow to Microsoft. As we all know, that didn't exactly work out as planned… Today, some people love JavaScript, others hate it, and some just make fun of it. But the truth is, the modern web simply wouldn't exist without it!

Over the years, JavaScript has gone through countless revolutions. Its capabilities today are almost incomparable to what the language could do back in the 1990s. There's just one tiny problem… Every change to the language has to take into account the fact that millions of websites out there still rely on old JavaScript behavior. And some of those websites will probably continue running that code until the end of time.

So, well, JavaScript's weirdness is probably here to stay forever! 😂

After quite a long break, I've decided to bring back my once-popular JS WTF series. For a very simple reason. I'm on my way back from iJS Munich, and I still have two hours to kill at Frankfurt Airport… (don't ask). Not enough time to write a groundbreaking, deeply technical article. But definitely too much time to just sit here and stare at the wall.

So let's take a look at one of my favorite JavaScript constructions:

Yes, you read that correctly. Under the right circumstances, if we add an empty object to an empty array in JavaScript, we get zero. And it makes perfect sense! 🤡

The first thing you need to know is that JavaScript doesn't necessarily interpret {} as an object in this situation! Depending on the context, the JavaScript parser can treat the expression as two completely separate things.

Consider this code at the beginning of a statement in a classic JavaScript script:

JavaScript can interpret it like this:

That's right. The first {} isn't an object literal at all. It's simply an empty block of code that does absolutely nothing. And the second part? Well, that's where the fun begins.

The expression:

is a classic example of type coercion , one of the things our wonderful language is famous for.

As you probably know, JavaScript is a dynamically and weakly typed language.

Dynamic typing means that variables aren't permanently tied to one type. You can assign a number to a variable and then replace it with a string, and JavaScript won't complain.

But there's more! JavaScript also performs implicit type conversions, which is one of the reasons it's often described as weakly typed. And sometimes those conversions produce rather… creative results.

item.title: I Earned a Seat at GitHub Universe. It'll Stay Empty, and That's Not Fair
item.content:encoded:
Originally published on 25 October 2026 at 06:44 UTC — 143 likes

I'm writing this to show how unfair the world we live in can be, sometimes ridiculously so.

This isn't the first time I've faced unfairness. It's happened more times than I can count, and by now I'm mostly numb to it. I don't really feel sad or angry anymore. I just keep going.

So this write-up isn't really for me. It's for people who are just starting out, or who aren't used to doing everything they possibly can, and even more, and still not getting what they deserve. I've seen so many people give up on their careers, their job searches, and their dreams because of moments like this. I was lucky to be resilient and stubborn enough not to let them break me.

Back in March, I won the biggest competition of my life, a challenge held by GitHub. I built Metal Birds Watch, an app I'm absolutely proud of. It's in maintenance mode right now, but it'll be back soon.

GitHub Copilot CLI Challenge Submission

I still don't know how I finished it. I was in severe pain the entire time. My neck, shoulder, and arm were absolutely killing me, and I could barely sit up straight. It was literal hell. But I pushed through and shipped it anyway.

So you can imagine how it felt to hear I'd won. And the prizes were amazing.

One of them was a one-year GitHub Copilot Pro+ subscription. I already had one, so GitHub offered me a very generous voucher for their shop instead. I asked them to donate that money to charity. It's the biggest charitable contribution I'd ever made, and I'm really proud of it.

The other prize was a ticket to GitHub Universe, the one I was looking forward to most.

Everything was going great.

That lasted until a month or two ago, when I found out I wouldn't be able to attend. The reason is absolutely ridiculous. Sometimes I catch myself laughing hysterically at the sheer level of this utter BS. But the world is a weird place right now. A very, very weird place.

I won't go into the exact reasons, but remember this: where you are in the world matters, especially at this point in history. It can affect your career, your life, everything. Don't be naive about it. No matter how successful you are, how good you are, or whether you do literally everything right, external factors don't give a damn.

One more thing I'm really annoyed about: the ticket is going to waste, and nobody can use it. I reached out to GitHub twice to ask whether I could transfer it to someone else, but I haven't heard back. I get it, they have a massive conference to run, so they're too busy to respond my emails, but still, I would've loved to give it to someone and make their day. It is what it is. I'm still infinitely grateful to GitHub for what they have done, I love you folks!

Nothing, really. Like I said, it's bad, but I've been through much worse, and I can handle this. I have way too much on my plate anyway, so I don't even have time to dwell on it.

For me, knowing I gave it everything I had, and more, is enough. Regretting that you didn't give it your all would feel far worse than this nonsense.

This write-up is mainly for people who give up the moment something doesn't go their way. Be stubborn. Focus on what you can control. Play the long game. You might lose a round, but that doesn't mean you've lost the match.

That's what I've always done, and it played out pretty well for me. So I'm just going to keep doing it. I might get things the hard way, but one way or another, I'll get them. I've lost rounds before. I've never lost the match.

The seat stays empty this year. It won't stay empty forever. I promise you that.

Let's stay connected!

item.title: AI Fatigue? Yea I know.
item.content:encoded:
Originally published on 13 October 2026 at 14:57 UTC — 172 likes

I don't know how to start this off really haha. Though to be fair, everyone is talking about AI ranging from building projects with AI, news about AI, dev.to articles about AI, and so on.

Though the more I see articles talking about AI, the more I felt like it's no longer interesting anymore. There is so much articles that is related to AI (ignore the part where I posted about making a portfolio in relations to AI) to the point where I want something... different.

I remember having discussions with various people on dev.to where back then there use to be articles that were very interesting such as CSS Tips, Resources every developer should know, etc. I can tell it was interesting back then because I visit that time. How? (I just find articles before 2022). There were so much variety of articles to look into and it gives the reader a lot of choices.

Today, most of the time I see articles talking about:

Topics in MCP

An app someone use AI to build it

Tokens

Models

Machine Learning

This is based on my experience by simply looking at the front page. Don't get me wrong, MCP is important and so is someone building an app using AI in some sense and talking about their process. The problem is that almost everyone is doing it to the point where it's hard to find an article that stands out from the rest.

It also gets difficult for people, like me, to find articles that are easy to understand because in most cases, articles talking about AI tend to be complex.

Do I mention "AI" in my articles, yes. I talk about AI and I fit into this category. However, I try not to talk about AI most of the time and focus on other aspects. In other words, not making AI the main focus.

For instance, on my last article, I talked about the reasons of creating a portfolio in the age of AI. I mainly talk about how you can structure your portfolio and use AI as a tool. The main highlight is talking about making your portfolio in the age of AI and how it's still relevant in this market.

Before you ask, yes, it gave me fatigue even reading my own article on it. However, this is expected.

If you are lucky enough, you can find an article that talks about anything not related to AI at all. However, there will always be some mention of AI whenever you read an article on dev.to or in any social media platform.

AI has becoming a discussion that seems unavoidable because AI plays a critical role whenever we are developing an app or how some companies using AI. AI is rapidly growing in a rate where it is hard to catch up for not only us developers, but for the general public as well. There are still some discussions about AI art and the legality of it to this day as it becomes much harder to distinguish.

It's everywhere. There is no escape from it and I don't know if it's even possible to escape from this fatigue. My fear is if we all know AI and if we remove AI from the equation from our lives, what do we truly know?

The question is never "how we differentiate topics between AI and non-AI?". we should all be asking: "What will we expect content to look like beyond AI?"

I would love to hear from you if you are experiencing this in the comments. If there is a solution to this, feel free to share this as well. Take care :D

item.title: Every Software Developer Has Blamed…
item.content:encoded:
Originally published on 8 October 2026 at 06:52 UTC — 164 likes

I got back from FrontKon in Prague today (well, technically yesterday, since I'm publishing this tomorrow), and I'm DEAD! 😂

The conference itself was fantastic, of course. Both my panel discussion and my talk went really well, and the Czech developer community is starting to feel like family. Greetings from your favorite senior software vývojářka ! 😀

I'll write my usual, more technical article next week. I want to approach the topic from a slightly different angle, so I need a bit more time for research. Meanwhile, flights from Gdańsk to Prague depart at the absolutely murderous hour of 6 AM, which means that at 3:30 AM today, I was still in Prague!

And since some of you have recently been asking for another installment of my "You're a Real Software Developer Only If…" series, here you go!

Who or what has every software developer blamed at least once? Here's my list!

Obviously, if the code is terrible, it's never our fault. Someone else must have messed it up. A colleague from our team, someone from another team, or the developer who worked on the project before us.

Quite often, though, that "other developer" turns out to be ourselves from six months ago. 😅

Because the processes are terrible, the standards are nonexistent, and management clearly has no idea what they're doing. The poor developer has been thrown into this corporate machine and is now forced to fight an endless battle against the system.

Things get a little awkward when you're self-employed and your company consists of… well, you. xD

The application could be just six months old, and somehow there will already be legacy code somewhere. And naturally, that legacy code is responsible for every bug, every delay, and every missed delivery deadline!

It's buggy! It's unpredictable! It's missing half the features we need!

If I wrote my own framework, now THAT would be something! And why haven't I done it yet? Well, I never promised anyone I would! 😅

Let's be real: our jobs would be so much easier and more enjoyable if it weren't for that annoying client who keeps asking for things and complaining about everything. 🤣

This is personally my first suspect whenever something goes wrong. If something doesn't work, it MUST be the fault of whoever wrote the backend.

I mean, come on. Are you seriously suggesting that something could possibly be wrong with MY code???

And this is exactly what backend developers think about the frontend whenever someone reports a bug.

Yes, yes, I know. In the age of AI, many of us have become full-stack developers, whether we wanted to or not. But deep down, our hearts will always belong a little more to one of those "ends." ☺️

Obviously. They're either too vague, poorly written, or based on some completely ridiculous idea invented by the stakeholders.

And even if the requirements are absolutely perfect, there's probably something missing from the documentation anyway. 😉

Come on, admit it. If you've never told someone to "clear your cache," can you even call yourself a software developer???

item.title: I'm Not on the DEV Team. I Still Debugged Their Missing Badges From Public Code. (And My First Test Was Wrong.)
item.content:encoded:
Originally published on 24 October 2026 at 18:12 UTC — 145 likes

I’m not on the DEV team. I don’t have an admin panel, production database access, or internal Slack. Everything I know about how DEV works comes from reading the public forem/forem repository. 🕵️‍♂️

Today, that was enough to diagnose why nobody on DEV was receiving multi-commit contributor badges, ship the service fix upstream, and get a "Thank you for this" and merge from @benhalpern Sir himself. 🚀

The 4x DEV Contributor Club badge: "Awarded for 4+ merged commits to Forem — Thank you so much for your contributions!"

It also taught me a humbling lesson about tests that pass for the wrong reason. 🧪

Over the past few days, I went on a contribution sprint in forem/forem and merged four pull requests:

#24003 — Docs: fix broken Kamal TOC anchor and index missing guides

#24056 — A11y: remove duplicate aria-describedby attributes in admin forms

#24094 — A11y: remove dangling aria-describedby references in creator settings

#24095 — Views/Liquids: quote src and add missing alt in user_subscription tag

My 1x ( dev-contributor ) badge showed up right away after PR #1. ✅

When PR #4 merged, I knew from config/schedule.yml that BadgeAchievements::BadgeAwardWorker runs every hour at :20 past the hour ( cron: "20 * * * *" ). I checked GitHub’s Contributors API ( /repos/forem/forem/contributors ) and confirmed my account was sitting on page 2 with contributions: 4 . Because Forem sets Octokit.auto_paginate = true , the worker was definitely reaching page 2.

One hourly cron passed. Then two. Then three. Still no 4x-commit-club badge. 💀

Me at :20 past the hour, every hour, refreshing my profile like it owes me money.

Instead of refreshing my profile for another 24 hours, I cracked open app/services/badges/award_contributor_from_github.rb . 🔍

Here is how Badges::AwardContributorFromGithub looked on main :

When I compared award_single_commit_contributors (which awarded my 1x badge) against award_multi_commit_contributors (which handles 4x, 8x, 16x, and 32x), three bugs jumped right off the screen:

Each key in BADGE_SLUGS is resolved via Badge.id_for_slug(slug) . If a slug in the production badges table doesn't match the hardcoded constant, id_for_slug returns nil . The service called .compact on the resulting hash and moved on. No error. No log line. Just a badge tier that quietly vanishes into the void. 👻

Because Forem only exposes resources :badges, only: [:index] without public /badges/:slug show routes, you can't query individual badge slugs directly. However, inspecting the public dev.to/badges catalog gave me a massive clue:

Badge #423 on /badges : Title: 4x DEV Contributor Club Description: 4x-commit-club

item.title: Congrats to the Kaggle Benchmarking Challenge Winners!
item.content:encoded:
Originally published on 5 November 2026 at 21:12 UTC — 100 likes

A few weeks ago we teamed up with Kaggle to ask a deceptively simple question: how do you actually know whether a model is any good at the work you do? The Kaggle Benchmarking Challenge asked you to stop reading someone else's leaderboard and build your own.

You did not hold back. Submissions measured whether models notice their "practice" hacking target is a real company's live system , whether they can reproduce the exact hash input for Spain's VeriFactu invoice ledger or just invent one , whether small local models hold their ground against fake authoritative notes buried in untrusted documents , and plenty more. Nearly every one of them started from something specific the author already knew was hard, which is exactly where the best evaluations come from.

Thank you to everyone who built, measured, and wrote. These benchmarks are a real contribution, and we hope you keep running them as new models ship.

Now, let's celebrate our winners!

Kaggle Benchmarking Challenge Submission

@jonathansolvesstuff asked 19 of the newest models a simple question: if it's 9 a.m. in Calgary in November, what time is it in Toronto? Alberta stopped changing its clocks in June, so the answer is 10:00, and every single model said 11:00. Their answer key comes from the public time zone database rather than anything written by hand, so the test can be run again each time that database updates.

Kaggle Benchmarking Challenge Submission

@nazar-boyko noticed that common advice about how much memory PHP arrays and Go goroutines use has quietly stopped being true. So they measured the real numbers themself across four versions of each language, then asked 12 models the same questions. The best models could quote the right release note but applied it to the wrong situation, and most reported high confidence even when they were wrong.

Kaggle Benchmarking Challenge Submission

@rustam335 asked ten models to write Blender scripts for four specific versions of the software, then actually ran every script in those versions to see what worked. Plenty of models produced code that ran fine while stating nothing had changed between versions. Making each answer list the changes it relied on is what exposed that gap.

Kaggle Benchmarking Challenge Submission

@kaichen_dev rebuilt 26 of the most expensive software failures in history as small code samples, then asked 13 models to review them as if the code hadn't shipped yet. The models flagged a problem almost every time, but frequently for the wrong reason, including spotting SQL injection in code that never touches a database. They also included disguised and already-fixed versions of each case, to catch models that merely recognize the famous bug and models that cry wolf on working code.

Kaggle Benchmarking Challenge Submission

@danielbutnar tested 43 models on two Romanian letters that look almost identical to their Turkish counterparts, where typing the wrong one is a common mistake. The models spell them correctly when the input is clean, but copy the wrong letter back about a third of the time when the input has it wrong. It even spread into words the models chose themselves, and their one-sentence fix for Romanian promptly broke Turkish, where the other letter is correct.

Each of our five winners will receive:

$500 USD

DEV++ Membership

Exclusive winner badge

All participants with a valid submission will receive a completion badge on their DEV profile.

The Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge is live! Build an experience that responds to real-time human signals captured through a camera. $3,000 in prizes across ten winners.

item.title: Don't Be a Proxy Between Me and Your AI
item.content:encoded:
Originally published on 22 October 2026 at 04:31 UTC — 150 likes

I've had this conversation more times than I'd like to admit.

I raise a technical question in a thread, a meeting, or a design review and someone responds with a long, well-structured, suspiciously balanced answer. It has headers in spirit if not in format, it covers 3 tradeoffs and ends with a neat recommendation.

I push back on one point. Silence for a minute, the kind where you can practically hear a browser tab switching. Then another equally polished paragraph appears, answering my pushback.

At some point it kinda gives: I'm not talking to a colleague. I'm talking to a chat window with a human-shaped copy-paste button attached.

please stop doing that, I'm practically begging you.

Let me say the obvious thing first. If I wanted to debate an AI, I'd debate an AI. I can type a question into ChatGPT, Claude, or whatever else is in vogue this week. It takes me 10 seconds, and I'd get to skip the middleman. Right now you're less a colleague and more a loading spinner with a LinkedIn profile.

When I bring a technical question to you, I’m asking for your judgment. What you’ve seen work, what you’ve watched fail, and what taught you the difference. I want to know which tradeoffs you’d accept, which assumptions you’d challenge, and why. That’s the experience I’m interested in hearing.

The moment you become a pass-through, I lose all of that. I'm getting generic output with your name on it, and you've added latency to the conversation without adding anything else. Congratulations, you've invented the world's slowest API wrapper.

This is the one that really gets me.

The pitch goes like this: in the AI era, the developer's job is to be the "architect". The AI generates the options, the human decides. You're like the guardrail, the one with taste.

Fine model. I think it's genuinely where a lot of the job is heading.

But a decision-maker who agrees with the AI's recommendation 99% of the time isn't deciding anything. That's a rubber stamp with a job title. If your "decisions" are indistinguishable from the model's default output, then you haven't added a layer of judgment, you've just added a layer of delay.

So here's a simple test: can you name a recent time you disagreed with the AI, and why? Not "I tweaked the formatting." A real disagreement, grounded in something the model couldn't know, like a constraint, a past incident, or a team preference.

If you can't, you're not the guardrail. You're the passenger and you didn't even pick the playlist.

I have a good, real example of this:

Someone messaged me on LinkedIn, saying they were interested in learning how I approach problems in distributed systems. I'll be honest: that's the kind of message that makes my day. A person wants to talk shop, and wants my thinking.

So I engaged. I walked through how I reason about failure modes and where I start when things go inconsistent and we went back and forth for a while.

Then I found out they'd been using an AI to debate me the whole time. They hadn't come to learn from me at all. They'd come to argue with me through a proxy.

And here's the thing: I debate AI every day. By choice, on my own terms, whenever I feel like it. That part is easy to get. What's rare is another human being who's actually willing to sit in the conversation, think out loud, be wrong in front of me, and push back with their own head.

If they'd just asked me their own half-formed questions, I'd have answered them all day.

item.title: This is my first HacktoberFest, and I don't know what to feel.
item.content:encoded:
Originally published on 2 November 2026 at 16:11 UTC — 133 likes

When reading this title, this may sound Netural...

Let me explain further. I do recommend reading this in full since I am a critical guy lol. If you want a short answer, I enjoy this HacktoberFest, but there are somethings that could be better based on my experience of a guy rarely participating haha. Take it as a grain of salt because of that lol!

HacktoberFest is an event I have heard many times over the years, but haven't really got the chance to join. Mainly because I simply don't have time and never had the courage to do Open-Source.

I heard about how HacktoberFest became a "SpamtoberFest" because of people creating low-quality Pull Requests on GitHub, which annoyed a lot of people in the Open-Source space.

With that said regardless, I was still excited into going into this event because I want to experience what it was like. I am not usually an event guy, but being part of HacktoberFest excites me.

When the event ended, I have mix feelings about it and I can't really pinpoint it really. Here are my thoughts.

To start, they remove Pull Requests count for this HacktoberFest. This makes sense because people are abusing the system of trying to make low effort pull requests just to get free stuff. It was a rational decision for sure and I can understand why. I feel bad for those who genuine make good Pull Requests at that time. It's basically our fault that there are those who ruin the fun for everyone.

To be fair, before the announcement, I was expecting some sort of "safe guard" where the team utilized AI and a human reviewer to review Pull Requests to determine if the PR is valid or not. Sure, it's a lot of work but it would make sense to use AI in the process.

However, seeing that they remove Pull Requests entirely is kind of disappointing because I want to get the feeling of making a PR, having that on my portfolio, and getting free stuff INCLUDING Stickers. That sounds like an accomplishment to me in this industry since it's important to showcase your contributions to recruiters to see you have work experience. It would be a nice alternative instead of just building projects.

Don't get me wrong, the current process is much better than simply pushing 2 PRs and you are done for this month. There was thought behind it and it allows developers to be more engaged by going into livestreams, building projects, etc. Though for me, it felt mostly empty because of how easy it was to get stickers by simply checking into livestreams and completing the basics to get Completionist.

You maybe asking, "what about projects?".

I didn't really feel conformable signing up to services that I won't use after the event. This is on me lol. I would have wish to negate my OCD for me to use these services freely, but I was pretty limited.

Note: Initially, I talked about how AI is not accessible because of hardware and cost in general regardless of free promotions you can claim. Also talked about how the projects are AI integrated focus and not building projects in general, with or without AI. I removed that chunk of the section because it's mostly a me thing and some things I was just completely wrong about. Just leaving a note here for transparency.

Note: Initially, I talked about how AI is not accessible because of hardware and cost in general regardless of free promotions you can claim. Also talked about how the projects are AI integrated focus and not building projects in general, with or without AI. I removed that chunk of the section because it's mostly a me thing and some things I was just completely wrong about. Just leaving a note here for transparency.

With all said, I still had fun surprisingly in this event. I get to see a lot of projects being built such as from @thomasbnt on his DEV feed and @dj29 projects I see time to time. I also got some stickers as well and recently became a completionist++!

Although getting to that status was easy, I didn't like how easy it was. There are some flaws to it for some stickers. For example, there was a Hack Day event at my city, but I didn't attend in person but was able to get the sticker for it if you submit a project. I would have wished there were more safe guards to it since I was able to not only check-in but submit my project as well without having to go in-person. Thus, getting a sticker for it.

Another thing is that I would have wish that being in that Competionist status allows us to at least get one free thing from it instead of entering a raffle. Maybe if you complete Completionist or Completionist++, you get a free t-shirt and you enter a raffle to get an Arduino (if you win of course). That makes much more sense. Maybe I am greedy idk lol, just comparing to previous events where you get more than just stickers haha

It's hard to say. There isn't really much because the team did what they could and they delivered! Though I do want one thing for next year that would make sense to me:

Bring back Pull Requests, but having some criteria to make the PR valid in some way. Bring in volunteers to review PRs and determine if it's valid. Both the Contributors and the volunteers get a reward for doing so.

Of course, there is more, but that's pretty much I can come up on my top of my head.

How Did I End Up Here?

Door #1: Let Go for Being Too Good

Door #2: The Interview I Tried to Write in C++

Door #3: The Call

The Door I'm Standing In Now

A few months ago, my DEV buddy @francistrdev invited me to join DEVengers. Of course, I accepted. It's a great team full of cool folks, they're all stars and it's a real honor to be among them.

The thing is, a team like this only stays alive if people keep showing up and writing. This is my first post under DEVengers, so I wanted it to be special: easy to read, but with some depth. Consider it the first domino. I'm knocking it over, and I fully expect the rest of the team to follow. (No pressure, folks.)

So here I am: thousands of followers, almost 50 articles, 2 hackathon wins, 6 Top 7 of the Week features, and that's only scratching the surface of what I've accomplished since I joined this amazing community.

You might think I've been creating content here for years. Nuh-uh. It's been just a year and a half since I started writing for real.

Here's the twist: I first heard about DEV back in 2017. Yes, some of you were probably still in high school. That was also around the time I started my professional software engineering career. A year later, in 2018, I registered.

So basically I bought the ticket in 2018 and boarded the train seven years later.

To be honest, there's no funny story about how I discovered DEV. No viral post, no friend or colleague dragging me in.

So instead, I'm going to do what Ted Mosby did in How I Met Your Mother TV show. He sat his kids down to tell them how he met their mother, and ended up telling them his entire life story first.

So grab a seat, fellow devs. This is the story of how I met DEV, and all the doors I had to go through before I finally stepped through this one.

Don't worry, though. Unlike Ted, I promise it won't take nine seasons.

Before I landed my first job as a junior software engineer, I worked in network and IT support while studying at university.

This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

"Every codebase has ghosts. In nearly every enterprise repo and open-source project, there is a haunted file marked with // DO NOT TOUCH: NOBODY KNOWS WHY THIS WORKS . When the original author moves on, their domain knowledge vanishes into the ether. The code slowly rots, dependencies decay, and fear prevents anyone from touching it."

"Every codebase has ghosts. In nearly every enterprise repo and open-source project, there is a haunted file marked with // DO NOT TOUCH: NOBODY KNOWS WHY THIS WORKS . When the original author moves on, their domain knowledge vanishes into the ether. The code slowly rots, dependencies decay, and fear prevents anyone from touching it."

For Week 4 of Hacktoberfest — celebrating Halloween and Día de los Muertos — I built GitSéance : an Open-Source AI Code Necromancer that turns the graveyard of legacy code into an interactive, grounded séance.

Instead of a generic linter, GitSéance coordinates The 4 Specialized Necromancy Agents :

💀 The Reaper Agent : Traverses the Git commit tree and file AST to identify abandoned, orphaned, and cursed code based on commit history, author turnover, and inline fear comments ( hack , black magic , do not touch ).

📊 The Oracle Agent (TabPFN-3.5) : Synthesizes a 7-dimensional forensic feature vector and feeds it into Prior Labs' TabPFN tabular foundation model to predict calibrated file mortality risk.

🔮 The Medium Agent (Google Gemma) : Channels the spirit of departed authors through Google's Gemma open-weight model ( gemma-4-26b-a4b-it ), generating first-person confessions, regret analyses, and modern revival blueprints.

🔍 The Searcher Agent (SerpApi) : Queries live 2026 package registries and security databases to find modern drop-in replacements for abandoned dependencies and audit CVE advisories.

These agents power Interactive Séance Capabilities :

💬 Conversational Séance (Interactive Ghost Chat) : Living developers can converse directly with the ghost in real time, asking why specific hacks were written and how to safely refactor them.

🔊 Neural Voice Deck (ElevenLabs) : Gives the spirit an audible voice via neural text-to-speech with a synchronized Web Audio API waveform visualizer.

🪦 Official Post-Mortem Autopsy Certificates : Generates downloadable vintage ASCII death certificates detailing cause of demise, bus factor, and TabPFN mortality score.

📊 7D Tabular CSV Forensic Exporter : One-click download of the complete tabular feature dataset for offline TabPFN model exploration and auditing.

🛡️ Live GitHub SVG Mortality Badges : Dynamic shields endpoint ( /api/badge/{owner}/{repo}.svg ) for embedding live repository mortality scores in README files.
